sections.overview: Biotodoma cupido is a South American freshwater cichlid of the geophagine lineage, native to the Amazon and Essequibo systems. Its only congener is B. wavrini; older names such as Geophagus cupido reflect past genus placements, not a separate species.
sections.identification: Adults reach about 12–13 cm. The oval, laterally compressed body usually has a dark stripe through the eye and a dark mid-flank spot, with fine greenish-blue streaks; regional colour forms vary and should not automatically be named as separate taxa.
sections.habitat: Its wide range includes clear, tannin-stained and seasonally changing rivers, floodplain waters and tributaries. It tolerates varied flow, from still backwaters to flowing channels, but accounts suggest it avoids the most torrential conditions.
sections.diet: It picks small bottom-dwelling prey such as insect larvae, tiny crustaceans and other invertebrates from the substrate. This benthic feeding is characteristic of the eartheater-like geophagine lineage, though it is not a specialised sand-sifter to the same degree as many Geophagus species.
sections.behavior: Outside breeding, it is generally a relatively peaceful cichlid and browses close to the bottom. Its behaviour and appearance may be compared with other geophagines, but the two Biotodoma species are the closest genus-level comparison: B. wavrini is a separate species, not a colour morph of B. cupido.
sections.reproduction: It is a biparental substrate spawner: the pair cleans a firm surface, lays and guards eggs, then protects the free-swimming fry. This differs from mouthbrooding in some cichlid lineages and resembles the parental care seen in several other geophagines.
sections.ecology: Seasonal flooding alters water depth, turbidity and current across much of its range, so populations encounter changing river and floodplain habitats. As a benthic predator it consumes small invertebrates and forms part of the food web for larger fishes.
sections.conservation: FishBase lists the IUCN Red List category as Least Concern, assessed on 30 November 2020. This global assessment does not establish that every local population is stable; population trends and species-specific threats remain poorly documented.
